Even the 8 core Ryzens are 105w, so they should technically work in the motherboard you chose. I was originally going to tell you to get that Gigabyte x470 that's on sale for $120 but the B450 is fine.

The idea is that every year or so, you would spend money on upgrades to work toward turning your system into a high end machine. It's a lot easier to spend $300 only on a CPU because that CPU works with the motherboard, RAM, etc you already have as opposed to spending $300 on a CPU in a new build. If you spent a little more on an x470 you could go a lot longer before upgrades. The new Ryzen CPUs will be using the same socket, so unlike with an Intel system you can still get away with building a system and expecting to put in a superior CPU in a year or two, or even three.

I've done this thing where I start with a cheap $500 budget system and slowly work it up towards something high end by upgrading it every year or so many times before. It's the best way to get a solid system without a huge initial investment.

X470 is not that great of an improvement from B450 except if you want some very specific things (SLI, 2 extra NVMe, x8 vs x6 PCIe Gen 3). A good B450 while support Ryzen 3000 just as well as an X470. Matter of fact, unless you are going high end with the X470 you are usually better off with B450 as the VRM cooling on the lower end ones is pretty bad and may not support any overclocking at all. An MSI B450 Tomahawk would be a much better choice than any Asrock except the Taichi and only costs around $110.

Higher end motherboards have better power delivery and support higher TDP CPUs. Those other features are nice, but an x470 would be warranted if you simply wanted to get into heavy overclocking (though Ryzen is boring to overclock) or you want to have the option for a better CPU later if future Ryzens end up going beyond 105w. Though I don't know how big of a deal that could end up being, 7nm 8 core Ryzen will probably be in the 65w TDP range.

Low end x470 motherboards do have worse VRM cooling, but they usually have better VRMs. Better VRMs are usually a little more efficient and don't get as hot.

AMD is just doing a very good job supporting multiple Ryzen CPUs on the same socket, and I think a lot of people view motherboards as disposable because there are a lot of people who grew up on modern Intel where sockets change every generation just because they can.
